newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algiers school bomb kills four, wounds 21.
newsitem.headline: Algiers school bomb kills four, wounds 21.

text.p: A bomb planted outside a high school killed three schoolgirls and a 12-year-old boy and wounded 21 people, many of them students, in a crowded Algiers suburb on Tuesday, Algerian security forces said.
The blast, the second attack on an educational centre within one week, came less than a month before general elections in the oil and gas producing country.
The security forces said in a statement carried by state media: "The dead are three schoolchildren and a child."
Witnesses had earlier reported that at least two people had been killed and a score of others, mainly pupils, wounded.
The dead schoolchildren were all girls, aged between 15 and 18, according to the statement. The child, a boy, was aged 12.
The authorities termed the bombing "a criminal act", the phrase generally used to accuse Moslem fundamentalists of attacks.
"Six among the wounded are in a serious state," the statement said. It added that the bomb was a "booby trapped parcel hidden under a car parked outside Frantz Fanon high school in Bab El-Oued."

Bab El-Oued is a popular working class suburb near the Casbah, the ancient heart of the Algerian capital, and was a focal point of radical Moslem unrest at the start of Algeria's violence five years years ago.
The suburb sheltered one of two mosques in which leaders of the now banned Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) used to preach fiery sermons and inspire their supporters to oppose the authorities.

There was no explanation as to why the bombing, like other previous attacks, should be carried out in a known bastion of fundamentalists. But several schoolgirls have been murdered for not covering their heads or for wearing Western dress.
Last Tuesday, a bomb wounded two girl students attending classes at a study centre at Bourouba in the Algiers suburb of El Harrach.

Three other bombs -- one under a train in Algiers late last month, and two at hotels in a thermal resort in Sidi Bouhanifia in northwest Algeria -- have killed another 36 people and wounded 43 in the past 11 days.

The upsurge in bombings, which had been eclipsed by the horror of a series of night-time massacres in isolated villages in which about 160 people were killed in four days in late April, coincides with increased political activity ahead of Algeria's first parliamentary election in over five years.
It was after the authorities in January 1992 cancelled the last general election, dominated by the FIS, that violence erupted. About 60,000 people have since been killed.

Diplomats have linked the rise in attacks to the approach of the June 5 general election for which the authorities say security will be increased to safeguard voters among Algeria's 29 million people.
President Liamine Zeroual sees the elections as a way to bring Algeria out of civil strife.
In February this year, Algeria announced a draconian ban on vehicles stopping in main streets and squares in the capital to try to thwart car bomb attacks.

Last Saturday, Zeroual said the government had defeated Moslem rebels. "Terrorism in our country has lost the war thanks to the courage and sacrifices of our people and its security forces," he told a public meeting.
